title: The Promises and Pitfalls of LLMs as Feedback Providers: A Study of Prompt Engineering and the Quality of AI-Driven Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT-4, can generate high-quality educational feedback and how prompt quality affects the usefulness and accuracy of that feedback. The authors address two questions: what kinds of prompts are needed to ensure high-quality LLM feedback, and how does LLM feedback compare with novice and expert human feedback in terms of quality dimensions such as concreteness, empathy, activation, and correctness.

The study develops a theory-driven prompt manual with eight prompt-quality categories and uses it to create three prompts of varying quality. These prompts are then used to generate feedback on a single learning goal in teacher education: a mathematics-related learning goal containing three formulation errors. The target population is in higher education, specifically pre-service teachers (novices) and educational experts such as teacher trainers, professors, and a headmaster. LLM feedback was produced repeatedly from the three prompts and coded quantitatively using a feedback-quality rubric; the highest-quality prompt was then used to collect human novice and expert feedback for comparison.

Results show that prompt quality strongly shapes LLM output: only the best prompt consistently elicited high-quality feedback, while a middling prompt sometimes increased hallucinated errors. Compared with novice feedback, ChatGPT-4 generally performed better across most feedback dimensions. Compared with expert feedback, ChatGPT-4 was comparable overall and even stronger in some subdimensions, especially explanation, questions, and specificity. The authors conclude that LLMs can be efficient and high-quality feedback providers in higher education, but only when guided by careful prompting and ideally supervised by human experts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative study with a clear coding and ANOVA-based design, but it is not an RCT or a learner-outcome trial. The study is well structured yet limited to feedback-quality judgments on a single task rather than direct educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong practical promise for faster, higher-quality feedback generation, but it does not test student learning or achievement effects. Because impact is limited to workflow and feedback quality outcomes, the educational impact remains plausible but unproven.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-4 used to generate feedback on a learning-goal writing task in teacher education, with prompt engineering varying in quality to test feedback quality and hallucination risk.
AI-generated feedback on a written learning goal, evaluated against human novice and expert feedback for specificity, explanations, questions, first-person perspective, valence, and factual errors.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-4 generated feedback much faster than expert humans: the model produced an average of 49 pieces of feedback in the time an expert produced one. The paper frames this as a substantial efficiency gain for feedback provision, although no formal time effect size was reported.
finding.measure: feedback production speed / time to generate feedback

finding.finding_summary: The LLM-based system reduced the burden of generating high-quality feedback relative to manual expert feedback, suggesting it could substitute for some routine feedback tasks. The study does not report a standardized effect size, but it provides direct comparative evidence that AI feedback is substantially faster to produce than expert feedback.
finding.study_size: n=60 LLM feedback instances for prompt comparison; comparison with 11 experts
